* Environmental Kuznets Curve (EKC) hypothesis remains central to examining CO2-economic linkages.
- Grossman and Krueger (1991) first proposed an inverted-U relationship between income levels and environmental degradation.
- Subsequent empirical studies across developing nations generally confirm EKC patterns, though threshold values vary considerably across regions.

* Renewable energy adoption significantly reduces carbon intensity of GDP growth.
- Soytas et al. (2015) found renewable energy consumption lowers CO2 emissions by 0.27 units per 1% increase.
- Solar and wind energy deployment demonstrates strongest negative correlations with industrial carbon output.

* Financial development channels exhibit complex, nonlinear effects on emission trajectories.
- Ang (2008) demonstrated financial deepening initially increases emissions before enabling clean technology investments.
- Stock market liberalization accelerates capital allocation toward environmentally sound production methods.

* Trade openness produces ambiguous environmental consequences depending on factor intensity.
- Antle and Bae (1998) documented pollution haven effects among low-income exporting nations.
- Technology transfer mechanisms associated with trade liberalization reduce carbon footprint per unit of output.

* Institutional quality determines effectiveness of climate policy in decoupling growth from emissions.
- Copelland and Taylor (2004) showed strong regulatory frameworks enable simultaneous GDP expansion and emission reduction.
- Corruption undermines environmental enforcement, weakening emission reduction outcomes regardless of economic performance.

* Structural economic transformation toward service-oriented economies yields substantial carbon reduction benefits.
- Stern (2013) argued deindustrialization represents most effective pathway for advanced economies.
- Digital economy expansion further accelerates decoupling through efficiency gains in logistics and manufacturing sectors.
